en: The Ritual for the Fire Hūṃ Offering:
Those who wish to practice the dharma of dhāraṇīs must first adorn the maṇḍala, ensuring that both the interior and exterior are clean and their robes are fresh and pure.
Free from all clamor and frivolous discourse, they should proceed according to the rules for recitation.
Thus, the four seasons must not be omitted.

If one season is omitted or if the rules are violated, one must begin the practice anew from the point of the violation or omission. Even if one intends to complete the full duration before the ritual procedure is finished, if even a single season is deficient, the entire undertaking is not accomplished; it is only when there is no transgression from beginning to end that the number of repetitions can be considered.

The number of recitations should follow the specific sequence of one's own tutelary deity (iṣṭadevatā) according to the respective section; once the count is completed, a natural state of realization will arise.

Alternatively, it may be feared that during the time of recitation, one violates the samaya, the mind lacks single-minded focus, or false conceptualizations arise; consequently, one cannot achieve resonance, and thus the pure realm does not immediately manifest before one.

Practitioners who specialize in cultivation must, according to their respective sections, make offerings to the best of their ability every month; for to lack offerings is not to be in accordance with one's section. These are as follows:

the fifteenth day for the Tathāgata Section, the fourteenth day for the Bodhisattva Section, the eighth day for the Vajra Section, the fifth day for the Deva Section, and the fourth day for the Yakṣa Section.

For all methods of making offerings, one should prepare the altar food at the first rising of the sun: sweet, fragrant, and crisp cakes; fine foods with oil and fat; and steamed milk porridge and curd-rice flavored with ghee and honey. One should offer various exquisite delicacies according to one's means, arranging various types of sacrificial beans in separate dishes.
When preparing the food and when about to enter the maṇḍala, one should always employ the heart-mantra and the mudrā of Kuṇḍalī.
The mantra for consecrating all the offering implements is:
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ mṛta hūṃ khaṃ ṭaḥ. Recite this over each item three or seven times; by doing so, one will avoid having them stolen by flying rākṣasas.

If one does not apply focused attention (*manasikāra*), there will be much defilement through contact; the messengers (*dūta*) and others will fail to rejoice and will subsequently obstruct the accomplishment.

Now, for the binding of the boundary (*sīmābandha*) and the protection of the body, one must act with speed and must not hesitate or waver, for fear that the swift-moving *kumbhāṇḍa* yakṣas might come to harass and disturb one. Therefore, when performing the binding and protection as well as the offerings, one must be extremely well-prepared and the proceedings must be rapid.

When making offerings, one must first bathe and purify oneself; outside the ritual arena (*maṇḍala*), sprinkle the body with scented water. Then, recite the syllable "HŪṂ" three times. Immediately form the *vajra-muṣṭi* (vajra-fist) with the right hand and visualize the assembly of holy beings filling the ritual arena, like successive reflections that do not obstruct one another. Then, prostrate three times and recite the outer ritual manual nine times.
Next, recite the mantra of Mahācakra-vajra twenty-one times; this is the method of confession.
With vajra-pañjali joined and both knees touching the ground, next visualize the syllable “HŪṂ” (or “RAṂ”) incinerating the world until it is like dust.
Next, visualize the syllable *Haṃ*, which is like a black wind blowing violently to purify [the field] so that it is free of all dust.
Next, visualize the gate of the syllable *Vaṃ*, imagining it to be as clear and translucent as milk-water, shining like a mirror.

Furthermore, above that, visualize the gate of the syllable *Su* forming Mount Sumeru; beneath the mountain, the Ocean of Milk spreads throughout the Dharma-realm; upon the mountain, the plateau is level with fruit-bearing groves in full bloom, where the waters and trees are pure, fragrant, and brilliantly radiant.

Next, holding the incense burner and burning incense, one should cultivate the visualization: upon Mount Sumeru, in a vast palace of a hundred jewels, with boundless jeweled pillars and jeweled spires from which banners hang, there is a crescent moon atop a jeweled pillar. Upon the moon is a *māṇikya* jewel, and rows of *kiṅkiṇī* nets are spread throughout, interlaced between them;
these so-called "Indra-nets" are all made of jewels, each jewel reflecting the others in a brilliant, translucent radiance.
Furthermore, one contemplates that the syllable *A* (*𑀅*) forms a *stūpa*.

Again, one should visualize the sacred stupa becoming the Great Sun Tathāgata (Vairocana), seated in the center of a precious lotus flower within the central hall, sitting cross-legged. Around the four sides, billions upon billions of lotus flowers are arrayed; within each flower sits a holy being, namely the Buddhas of the ten directions who have come to bear witness. Bodhisattvas and Vajrapāṇis stand as guards before and behind, while the multitudes of the Two Vehicles are immeasurable and boundless, and devas and nāgas fill the space beyond limit.
In the space above, the sublime sounds of elegant music, pure and refreshing to the heart, extensively performed the work of the Buddha;
that is to say, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens played exquisite and wondrous music.

On all sides of the assembly, auspicious vases, *argha* vessels filled with fragrant water, conch shells, and earthenware bowls, along with clouds of incense and a profusion of precious flowers, fell in a chaotic rain. Fragrant food and rare delicacies overflowed from jeweled platters; exquisite fruits and extraordinary juices possessed intense and potent flavors. Robes of precious fabric trailed across the central stage, their radiance dazzling, while pearl torches shone like the sun, their myriad colors reflecting one another.

Having performed such mental visualization, one next proceeds to the recitation. According to the ritual, one should briefly recite the mantra of the principal deity one hundred and eight times, or twenty-one times.
Next, one consecrates the food and drink with the mantra of the consort Ākāśadhātvīśvarī and other mantras such as the Mahāvidyā; this is termed the "Dharma-offering."

Having completed the offerings, perform the ritual of dismissal one hundred and eight times according to the rules for recitation; as for the *hūṃ*-method for the fire, maintain it and follow the rules for recitation exactly as in the previous method.
Furthermore, there are briefly four types of fire rituals (*homa*):
first, the *śāntika* rite. One should face north;

the hearth should be constructed as circular, and all ritual implements should be white. Generally, Samantabhadra is the presiding deity, though each family (*kula*) has its own corresponding deity. This is called the pacification of calamities and the extinguishing of sins.
The robes, painted images, and all other items shall be entirely white. Second is the Puṣṭika rite:

one should face east and perform the ritual using a square hearth; all the offering implements shall be yellow. With Avalokiteśvara as the primary deity, this is called the accomplishment of fulfilled wishes and all superior matters.
Third is the *ābhicāruka* rite. One should face south;
the ritual hearth is triangular, and all the offering implements are entirely red. For this, Vajrapāṇi is generally the presiding deity.
Fourth is the *pracaṇḍa-kalpa*. One should face west;

the hearth should be octagonal like the petals of a lotus flower, and all the offerings should be the color of purple sandalwood. This is called the rite for seeking respect and affection when wishing to see a Great Being.

The four hearths mentioned previously are each one cubit square by the small measure (one chi eight cun), with a depth of half that; at the bottom of each hearth, a single-pronged pestle is fashioned from clay, measuring eight finger-widths in length.
Regarding the circular hearth and the octagonal hearth, one should fashion them as the *karmavajra*, that is, the ten-spoked vajra.

The rims of the hearths should all be made in three tiers; starting from the inner height and moving outward, they gradually decrease, with each tier being four finger-widths wide, totaling twelve finger-widths in width. Upon the edge of the rim, one may draw flowers at will; if one is unable to draw them, one should visualize them as being present.
The firewood, incense, flowers, and other materials should all be placed on the right side.

Three times each day—at sunrise, at midnight, and during the final watch of the night—one should perform one hundred and eight recitations for each occasion. As for the firewood, use grain-tree wood, *nyagrodha* wood, mulberry wood, cypress wood, pine wood, and so forth.

Each time the wood is split and pared, it should be as thick as a middle finger and twelve finger-widths long; it must be free of nodes and the fibers must be straight. One should select a small tree of medium color, avoiding old, withered trees or those infested by insects.

When gathering [the materials], one must observe whether there are auspicious signs before collecting them. If one sees an unfilial son, a person with physical disabilities, a woman, or malevolent birds and beasts, one must not collect them at all, but should instead seek them elsewhere.
For each session, one hundred and eight pieces [of incense] are used; these are placed in a stack on the right side of the furnace, arranged with a railing-like border.

Regarding the method for powdered incense (*vilepana*): take one and a half *jin* of white sandalwood, grind it with pure water upon a stone, and further grind it together with a small amount of agarwood (*kālāguru*).
Furthermore, take a small portion of saffron and grind it finely with agarwood;
also take a small portion of camphor—or if camphor is unavailable, saffron alone may be used, as is also acceptable for sandalwood.
The *argha* ritual:

Using water filtered for purity, take a small amount of scented ointment (*vilepana*) and drop it into the pure water; add exquisite, pure flowers to this water as well, ensuring they are refined, and place the mixture in a new, clean porcelain bowl.

Furthermore, take one bottle of scented water and place it before the seat, directly in front of the incense burner, for fire-offering. With the left hand, hold a ritual mallet (vajra) and press down upon it.
The method for preparing the incense pills is as follows:

two *liang* of agarwood (*agaru*), eight *liang* of *shenxiang* (a light fragrance), three *liang* of *suhexiang*, one *liang* of *xiangfuzi*, two *liang* of *ansixiang*, two *liang* of *xunluyang*, one *liang* of *qingmuxiang*, two *liang* of *qiantang*, and two *liang* of white sandalwood (*candana*).
Take one part of kakkola (camphor), one part of turmeric, and one part of musk; grind these three substances together in one place. Take two *liang* of nakha (claw-fragrance);

wash it with water decocted from *janghu* (a type of plant) and fry it with honey until dry, then grind it separately. To the right, combine these ingredients with refined honey in the appropriate proportion; finally, add the three flavors beginning with kakkola. If these are difficult to obtain in the local region, substitute them as available.
The Method for Preparing Incense:

Take two *liang* each of *gan-song*, *ling-ling-xiang*, and *kong-qiong*; one *liang* of *ding-hiang*; two *liang* of *ze-lan*; one *liang* of *chen-xiang*; and three *liang* of high-quality *qian*. Grind all the above ingredients together.

Take two *liang* of *suhaka*, half a *liang* each of *kakkola*, *kuṅkuma*, and musk, place them separately in silk bags, and add white mustard seeds, which are to be kept apart from the other ingredients. When all the grains have been prepared, [place these items within].
The method for the three sweets:
butter, honey, and curdled milk are each counted as three or four portions per session; the curdled milk is reduced by half and mixed together, all contained in a single copper basin.
The method for the five grains:
Rice grains, flower-shaped rice cakes, polished rice, and oil, boiled together and dyed purple, red, yellow, or other colors, are called "rice-flower offerings" and placed in one vessel.
Sesame seeds, mung beans, red beans, wheat, and non-glutinous rice—these are mixed together and placed in another separate vessel.
The method for regularly preparing incense is as follows:
use camphor; if it is unavailable, one may use one grain of white cardamom, or if that is also unavailable, clove.

For the fire-offering, the incense-burner offering, and the offerings of dried dates, chestnuts, yellow granulated sugar, and rock honey, prepare whatever materials you can afford according to your means.
First, the offerings, invocation, boundary-binding, and protection of the body are performed exactly as listed above.
At the time of binding the boundary, add the earth stakes, the vajra wall, the vajra net, the vajra flames, and the mantras and mudrās of the Immovable One and the sword.

At the time of invocation, invoke each of the eight directional Dharma-protecting Heavenly Kings individually, reciting [the mantra] seven times for each while employing the Vajra-invocation mudrā. First, offer the three flavors to the Fire Deity, followed by three ladles of the five grains, powdered incense, guggulu incense, and so forth. Thereafter, direct the mind to universally make offerings to the noble assemblies of the five families, reciting the Great Extensive Mantra, the Gaganagañjā-vidyārājñī Mantra, and others.

Next, recite the mantra of the *iṣṭadevatā*. Dip both ends of the firewood into the three substances; reciting the mantra once, cast it into the hearth. Furthermore, one must maintain a settled mind and remain composed, without any haste or agitation.
Next, when the offering of firewood is complete, one shall burn the five grains. At each occurrence of "Svāhā," add the specific prayer for the rite to be performed—for example:

"For such-and-such a person, śāntika svāhā. Recite the mantra of the Heart of the Heart of Kuṇḍalī while sprinkling scented water over all the objects, the fire, and so forth; at the time of sprinkling the water, chant the Kuṇḍalī Heart-to-Heart Mantra.
The mantra for first lighting the fire is:

*Oṃ bhujaṅga-lā*. Recite this twenty-one times. Fan the fire with a fan; do not blow on it with your mouth. If the fire is to be used within the temple precincts, one must not take fire from a layperson’s household that has been used for cooking or roasting meat and pungent foods; otherwise, one must separately drill for fire, and even then, one must not blow on it with the mouth.
Use two incense burners: on the right side of Kuṇḍalī, burn pellet incense and agarwood; on the left side of Kuṇḍalī, burn guggulu, or frankincense, or bdellium.

The quantity of the offering materials should vary according to the circumstances, being abundant or meager as appropriate; if abundant, one must not burn too much, and if meager, one must not let them be deficient.

If one is unable to provide the offerings, one may simply extend the mind to make vast offerings during the final watch of the night and at dawn; it is also permissible to recite extensively the *Gaganāyā* (Space Queen) mantra.
When throwing wood to kindle the fire, one should observe the characteristics of the flames. Regarding the color of the fire, the dharmas require it to be white, yellow, or red;

if it is black or blue, both are unfavorable. Furthermore, one should listen to the sound of the fire: sounds like music that are pleasing to the mind are auspicious, whereas sounds like those of pigs, dogs, donkeys, mules, or owls are inauspicious.

Moreover, a flame that rises with a flickering, smooth flow is auspicious; if it smolders with thick, oppressive smoke that assails the person, it is inauspicious, as is a fire that emits crackling bursts and scatters sparks.

The characteristics of an auspicious firewood are that it does not cause heat; its pieces must be straight and of even thickness, washed thoroughly with scented water, and each must be at least twelve finger-widths long. The mantras for the Eight Celestial Deities and the mantra for the Fire Deity have already been recorded separately in full.
If the color of the fire is auspicious, one may burn the sacrificial cakes (*bali*) in the hearth to perform the offering; if the color of the fire is unfavorable, one need not burn them.

The fire offering (*homa*) shall be limited to seven days, though if circumstances prevent it, three weeks (twenty-one days) is also permissible. This method of fire offering is intended to support one's recitation (*japa*), causing swift accomplishment.
One should also not perform practices such as *abhicāruka* (malevolent rites), for doing so obstructs the great conditions necessary for attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Furthermore, regarding the realms encountered during visualization or within dreams, these have been explained extensively in the sūtras and are not detailed here.

If the fire ritual (*homa*) is still not swiftly accomplished, one should immediately perform the double recitation of the *kulamātṛ-mantra*. If after another twenty-one days the *kulamātṛ-mantra* has been added yet one's original aspiration is not fulfilled, one should seal a stūpa and recite [the mantra] one thousand times daily; after another twenty-one days, one’s aspiration will surely be realized.

The stūpa-seal is one cubit in length; one must also personally assess the extent of one's own strength and the subtlety of one's karmic practice. Although there are prescribed recitation counts, if the maintenance of the rite is coarse and negligent, it is not a corresponding practice. One must ensure that the three karmas are harmonious and supple and that the ritual methods are thoroughly matured. One must personally observe whether one accords with the principle; when one naturally invokes the sages, they appear like reflections manifesting in a clear mirror.
The Ritual Manual for the Fire Hūṃ Offering (Homa)
